Summarize the following article in 5 bullet points for an executive audience:

Remote work has reshaped commercial real estate in ways few predicted. Office vacancy rates in major US cities climbed above 20 percent in 2024, the highest level in decades, as companies downsized their footprints and adopted hybrid schedules. Landlords responded with concessions: months of free rent, generous build-out allowances, and shorter lease terms. Meanwhile, demand shifted toward smaller, higher-quality buildings with modern ventilation, flexible floor plans and amenities such as fitness centers and rooftop space. Older buildings, especially those built in the 1970s and 1980s, have struggled the most; some owners have handed the keys back to lenders rather than fund expensive renovations. Several cities are experimenting with office-to-residential conversions, though the economics are difficult: deep floor plates leave interior spaces without windows, and plumbing must be rerouted for dozens of new kitchens and bathrooms. Banks with heavy exposure to commercial mortgages have tightened lending, which in turn makes refinancing harder for owners whose loans come due. Some analysts expect the adjustment to take most of the decade, while others argue that a return-to-office push by large employers will stabilize demand sooner than the market expects. Local governments face their own squeeze, because lower assessed values reduce property tax revenue that funds schools and transit. Retailers and restaurants that depended on weekday office workers have also felt the change, with foot traffic in central business districts still below pre-2020 levels in most cities.

This query takes 40 seconds on a 200M-row events table. Explain the plan and rewrite it to run in under a second. We can add indexes but can't change the table layout.

```sql
SELECT u.id, u.email, count(*) AS n
FROM users u
JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.id
WHERE e.created_at > now() - interval '7 days'
  AND lower(e.type) IN ('purchase', 'refund')
GROUP BY u.id, u.email
HAVING count(*) > 3
ORDER BY n DESC
LIMIT 100;
```
